title: Stream-safe JSON escape + resume protocol for function & tool call payloads
creator: Rosa Martinez
description: Background: Our streaming API returns structured JSON objects for function/tool calls and structured outputs. In practice, downstream clients (SDKs, proxies, browser apps) receive partial token streams that can cut JSON objects mid-token or mid-string, and model retries or network reconnects can cause fragments to be replayed or missed. We need a resilient, minimal protocol that: 1) lets clients safely reconstruct complete JSON objects and arrays across arbitrary truncation boundaries, 2) encodes safe escaping for untrusted tool outputs, 3) supports idempotent resume/retry after transient errors, and 4) is backward-compatible with existing SDKs that expect newline-delimited JSON events.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Streaming payload format defined in a single-page spec and reviewed. 2) Server-side library implements chunk headers with offset and fragment flags and integrated in runtime-1.22. 3) JS/Python SDKs implement a robust reconstructor that passes fuzz tests for: truncated UTF-8, broken escape sequences, back-to-back fragments, and duplicated fragments. 4) Retries/resume flow avoids double-processing for function/tool executions by using idempotency token + sequence offsets. 5) End-to-end tests covering simulated network cuts show correct JSON reconstruction 99.99% of test cases.
design_notes:
Summary of proposed protocol: - Each streaming event remains a top-level record separated by a single newline (
) for backwards compatibility. - If a JSON object cannot be fully emitted in one tokenized chunk, we emit a small deterministic ASCII header prefix on the same line: "<RS><meta>" where <RS> is ASCII Record Separator (0x1E) to avoid colliding with normal text. The <meta> payload is a compact base64url-encoded header: {seq:<n>, offset:<byte_offset>, frag:0|1, checksum:<crc32>}. The header is encoded as bytes, then base64url, and surrounded by angle brackets to keep it human-readable. Example chunk: 
<PzE6YzoxLmQ=>{"partial": "..."} (actual chunk contains header then JSON fragment). - Server guarantees that every fragment for a logical event shares the same seq id and monotonically increasing offset. - Fragment payloads are raw UTF-8 slices of the JSON text (not token counts). - The client reconstructor maintains for each seq: a byte buffer, received offsets set (to detect duplicates), and expected next_offset. On receiving a fragment it validates checksum and places bytes at the offset; when a complete JSON object parses successfully, the event is emitted. - To handle escaped/unpaired surrogates and mid-codepoint truncation, the server will avoid splitting multi-byte UTF-8 codepoints by only slicing on codepoint boundaries where possible; the reconstructor must still be tolerant: it should treat invalid UTF-8 sequences by replacing them with the Unicode replacement character and proceed with parsing. - For tool/function-call outputs that include binary-like blobs (base64) or user-supplied content, servers must mark fragments with frag=1 until final; a final fragment has frag=0. - Resume behavior: upon reconnect client sends an idempotency resume request with last-good-seq and last-good-offset; server responds with any missing fragments starting from offset. If the server no longer has fragments, it can send a special control event: 
<RESEND_NEEDED><seq>:client must reissue the top-level request or accept a fallback text-only summary. - Backward compatibility: if a client does not implement the reconstructor and sees unknown 0x1E header, it ignores lines starting with 0x1E and falls back to best-effort tokenized text. - Safety: server strips or escapes control characters inside string values that could be used to smuggle additional 0x1E headers into fragments. We add a server-side sanitizer: any ASCII control byte in the output (0x00-0x1F excluding 	,
,) is replaced with \u00XX escapes before fragmenting. This avoids header injection.
tradeoffs: - Using 0x1E prefix is slightly non-standard but avoids changing existing newline-delimited semantics. - Offsets are byte-based for simplicity; this requires careful server slicing on UTF-8 boundaries but makes resume deterministic across language clients. - Adding a checksum increases header size but makes duplicate/damaged-fragment detection robust. - The approach requires server-side work to keep fragments for some retention window (configurable per request) which adds memory/disk costs. We prefer short retention with a clear fallback path to re-run or provide partial summary.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): implement header emitter in runtime that can be toggled per-model and per-route; enable for 10% of streaming requests for customers in QA environment. Phase 2 (SDKs): release JS/Python reconstructor libraries and add to SDK streaming parsers. Phase 3 (wider): opt-in runtime flag for all streaming structured outputs and document the resume protocol. Phase 4: consider making the protocol default if adoption metrics show reduced parsing errors. Monitoring: instrument fragment-reassembly success rate, checksum failures, resume requests, and resend-needed events. Metric names: streaming.fragments.reassembled, streaming.fragments.checksum_fail, streaming.resume.requests, streaming.resend_needed.count.
test_plan: Unit tests for header parsing and base64url decoding; fuzz harness that randomly truncates JSON strings, injects duplicate fragments, and corrupts bytes to ensure reconstructor recovers or fails gracefully. Integration tests running JS and Python SDKs against a simulated flaky network that cuts connections at random token boundaries. End-to-end runbooks for customers: steps to read partial results in the SDK, how to request resume from a particular offset, and fallback behaviors.
